title: What does the EU seafarer training directive require of shipping companies, and how is it checked in port?
description: Directive (EU) 2022/993 on seafarer training: company familiarization duties, revalidation, non-EU certificates and port State control, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Directive (EU) 2022/993 codifies STCW in EU law for seafarers on ships flying a Member State flag. Beyond requiring STCW-standard training, it makes companies responsible for crew certificates, ship-specific familiarization and refresher training, sets a five-year revalidation cycle and a two-year medical certificate, controls recognition of third-country certificates through the European Commission and EMSA, and lets port State control officers check certificates and detain ships for listed competence failures.
keyTakeaways: Directive (EU) 2022/993 was adopted on June 8, 2022 as a codification and replaced Directive 2008/106/EC from July 17, 2022.

Article 15 requires companies to ensure every seafarer holds an appropriate certificate, is familiarized with ship-specific duties and equipment, and has received STCW refresher and updating training.

Masters, officers and radio operators must revalidate at intervals not exceeding five years (Article 13), and seafarers' medical certificates last a maximum of two years, or one year under age 18 (Article 12).
A Member State can only endorse a third-country certificate after the Commission, assisted by EMSA, recognizes that country, generally within 24 months of the request.
Port State control under Articles 23 to 25 verifies certificates and safe manning, can require seafarers to demonstrate competence at their place of duty, and can lead to detention.
regulator: European Commission, assisted by the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA); maritime administrations of EU Member States
appliesTo: Seafarers serving on seagoing ships flying the flag of an EU Member State, excluding warships, fishing vessels, pleasure yachts not engaged in trade and wooden ships of primitive build
Shipping companies responsible for assigning seafarers to those ships
Maritime education and training institutions and the authorities that certify seafarers
Any ship, whatever its flag, in an EU port, for port State control of seafarer certificates

sections.heading: What is Directive (EU) 2022/993 and how does it relate to STCW?

blocks.text: [Directive (EU) 2022/993](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32022L0993) of June 8, 2022 "on the minimum level of training of seafarers" is a codification. Its recitals explain that Directive 2008/106/EC had been substantially amended several times and that "in the interests of clarity and rationality" it should be codified. Article 34 repeals Directive 2008/106/EC, and the [EUR-Lex record](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32022L0993) shows the repeal taking effect on July 17, 2022.

Article 3 requires Member States to ensure seafarers on their ships "are trained as a minimum in accordance with the requirements of the STCW Convention, as laid down in Annex I to this Directive". The technical training content is therefore STCW. This page does not repeat it; basic training, its four competence tables and the five-year refresher are covered in [STCW seafarer training requirements](/regulations/stcw-seafarer-training-requirements).

What the Directive adds is EU-level machinery: duties on companies that EU law can enforce, a common revalidation and medical regime, a Commission-run system for accepting certificates from outside the EU, and port State control rules tied to Directive 2009/16/EC. EUR-Lex's document record listed no amending directive when checked in November 2026.

sections.heading: What must shipping companies do under Article 15?

blocks.text: Article 15 makes Member States hold companies responsible for assigning seafarers in line with the Directive. Every company must ensure that:

items: Each seafarer assigned to its ships holds an appropriate certificate.
Its ships are manned in accordance with the flag State's safe-manning requirements.
Documentation and data on all seafarers, including experience, training, medical fitness and competence in assigned duties, are maintained and readily accessible.

On assignment, seafarers are familiarized with their specific duties and with all ship arrangements, installations, equipment, procedures and characteristics relevant to their routine or emergency duties.
The ship's complement can effectively coordinate in an emergency and in functions vital to safety or pollution prevention.
Seafarers have received refresher and updating training as required by STCW.
There is effective oral communication on board at all times, in line with SOLAS chapter V, regulation 14.

blocks.text: Article 15(3) adds a written-procedure duty: the company must give each master written instructions ensuring newly employed seafarers have a reasonable period to become acquainted with the specific equipment they will use and the ship-specific watchkeeping, safety, environmental and emergency procedures, and must designate a knowledgeable crew member responsible for giving them essential information in a language they understand. Article 15(4) requires familiarization training for those with specific duties on ro-ro passenger ships, taking into account STCW Code section B-I/14.

These duties sit alongside the familiarization duty in section 6.3 of the [ISM Code](/regulations/ism-code-personnel-and-training-requirements). A single familiarization procedure written to satisfy both is the usual approach for EU-flagged fleets.

sections.heading: How often must certificates and medicals be renewed?

blocks.text: Under Article 13, every master, officer and radio operator serving at sea, or intending to return after a period ashore, must at intervals not exceeding five years meet the medical fitness standards and establish continued professional competence under STCW Code section A-I/11. Masters and officers on tankers and on ships operating in polar waters must also establish continued competence for those ship types at intervals not exceeding five years.

Under Article 12, every seafarer holding an STCW certificate and serving at sea must also hold a valid medical certificate. Candidates must be at least 16, and certificates remain valid for a maximum of two years, or one year for seafarers under 18. Medical examiners must be practitioners recognized by the Member State.

Article 16 sets the fitness-for-duty rules that drills must respect: watchkeepers and those with designated safety, security and pollution prevention duties must have at least 10 hours of rest in any 24 hours and 77 hours in any seven days, and musters and drills must be conducted to minimize disturbance of rest. It also sets a blood alcohol limit of not more than 0.05 percent for those performing designated safety, security and marine environmental duties.

sections.heading: How are certificates from outside the EU recognized?

blocks.text: Through the Commission, not each Member State alone. Under Article 20, a Member State that wants to endorse certificates issued by a third country must ask the Commission to recognize that country, with a preliminary analysis of its STCW compliance. The Commission, assisted by EMSA, assesses the country's training and certification system and adopts an implementing act on recognition within 24 months of the request, or 36 months where major corrective action is needed. The requesting Member State may recognize the country unilaterally in the meantime.

Recognized countries are reassessed under Article 22 on a regular basis and at least within 10 years of the last assessment, using priority criteria that include port State control performance data and the number of endorsements issued. Under Article 21(8), if no Member State has issued an endorsement for a recognized country's certificates for more than eight years, the recognition is re-examined.

For crewing managers, Article 20(7) matters day to day: a Member State may allow a seafarer to serve for up to three months while holding a valid third-country certificate not yet endorsed by the flag State, provided documentary proof that an endorsement application has been submitted is kept readily available.

sections.heading: What can port State control officers check and detain for?

blocks.text: Under Article 23, any ship within scope, whatever its flag, can be inspected in an EU port to verify that every seafarer required to hold an STCW certificate holds one, or a valid dispensation or documentary evidence. Article 24 limits the routine check to certificates and safe manning, but if there are clear grounds, such as a collision or grounding, an illegal discharge, erratic navigation or a fraudulently obtained certificate, the officer may assess watchkeeping and security competence under STCW Code Part A, including by asking a seafarer to demonstrate competence at the place of duty.
Article 25 lists the only grounds under the Directive on which a ship may be detained, where they pose a danger to persons, property or the environment:

items: Seafarers without certificates, appropriate certificates, valid dispensations or proof of an endorsement application.
Failure to comply with the flag State's safe-manning requirements.
Navigational or engineering watch arrangements that do not conform to the flag State's requirements.
Absence in a watch of a person qualified to operate equipment essential to safe navigation, safety radio communications or pollution prevention.
Failure to provide proof of professional proficiency for duties assigned for ship safety and pollution prevention.
Inability to provide sufficiently rested persons for the first watch and subsequent relieving watches.

blocks.text: Several grounds are evidence questions. A ship that cannot produce proof of proficiency for an assigned duty can be detained even if the seafarer is in fact competent, which is why [audit-ready training records](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) matter at sea as much as ashore.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each Article 15 company duty to the STCW competence and the ship-specific familiarization items that discharge it, and records certificate, medical and revalidation dates against each seafarer. The output is the evidence set a port State control officer asks for under Articles 24 and 25, available before the ship arrives.

faqs.q: Is Directive (EU) 2022/993 a new set of training requirements?
faqs.a: No. It is a codification of Directive 2008/106/EC, which had been substantially amended several times, and it repealed that Directive from July 17, 2022. The training content remains STCW, as laid down in Annex I. Its distinctive parts are company duties, revalidation and medical rules, third-country recognition and port State control.

faqs.q: How long is a seafarer's medical certificate valid under EU law?
faqs.a: A maximum of two years, or one year if the seafarer is under 18, under Article 12 of Directive (EU) 2022/993. Candidates must be at least 16 and examined by a medical practitioner recognized by the Member State.

faqs.q: Can a seafarer with a non-EU certificate work on an EU-flagged ship?
faqs.a: Only if the issuing country has been recognized through the Article 20 procedure and the flag Member State has endorsed the certificate. A Member State may allow service for up to three months while an endorsement application is pending, if proof of the application is kept readily available.

faqs.q: Can port State control require a seafarer to demonstrate competence?
faqs.a: Yes, where there are clear grounds, such as a collision, grounding, illegal discharge or unsafe navigation. Article 24(3) allows the assessment to require the seafarer to demonstrate the relevant competence at the place of duty, including the response to emergency situations.
